utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today, again, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away due to his official function. Today, we are going to finish your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday -- or, rather, on Friday, we touched upon relationships within the party and how it functioned, so now I would like to put some documents to you. I believe that you attended this plenary meeting of the Main Board of the Executive Board, and other officials, on the 14th of February, 1992, in the Holiday Inn, when the negotiations on the transformation of Bosnia were already underway. Could we please have P12. It has to do with this decision, D1222, about the election of the Executive Board that we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we had frozen the work of the party and that it was only at the 17th plenary session in Jahorina, held on the 17th of February, we resumed our party activities because many parties had been established in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, that is quite correct. We had major problems with the membership because they were asking that the party operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention now to my words that you can see here, where I say: "We hope that the MPs are strengthening their activities in the municipalities." It's towards the bottom of this page. Let us have a look at the English page. It's somewhere there. It's page 2, actually, in English. Yes, page 2. So: "We hope that the MPs are getting more active in municipalities, because as we concluded the last time, our representatives' authority for us party and parties are service to the elected people, to the people, and to people elected by the people to carry out the political will of the people." So: "Party officials are not authority to us." Can we have the next page in Serbian, though: "Authority for us are, first of all, the representatives, then representatives in municipal assemblies and others." Was it your experience that this was a well-founded position that we did not deviate from?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is quite correct, we did not deviate from this. We were at the service of our own people. We were the servants of our own people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I have page 7, please, in Serbian. And in English, it is page 9, and then we'll move on to page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the top, it says: "I have to say that in many municipalities, the party is not doing anything." And then towards the bottom, in the last quarter, it says: "Another problem that cropped up is the problem of alienation of the authorities from the party. We cannot allow that. Presidents of municipalities, presidents of municipal boards, do not really hold in high regard the MPs that they are supposed to hold in high esteem. They are a member of the Joint Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our policy --" The last words down there, can we have it scrolled up: "Our policy is charted not in the Executive Board, but the Political Council and the Club of Deputies." Is that something that was well known as well and a position that was not deviated from?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite correct, and I'm sure that they are -- told the investigators once, or perhaps even twice, that the Club of Deputies, headed by Vojo Maksimovic, was a very important link in the chain in the Serb authorities and that it had major influence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 12 in Serbian and 20 in English. I'm afraid that I haven't provided the right page references. Three pages from here. In Serbian, it's the third page from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Where it says: "... 500.000 Serbs, a million Serbs, are staying outside the Krajina and we have to reach an agreement. If this policy is no good, that is what the Main Board must conclude today, that it is not good, that it leads us nowhere, that it's not been realised, that none of the goals have been achieved, and then we should change the leadership. I will personally be grateful to you. They are going to give me a medal. I am going to be an honorary member, I don't know what, because I was the first president of the party and I'm going to be happy and grateful if we move on to another policy. And if there is another policy and if you are offering it, and we are not implementing it, then we deserve to be replaced by you." And towards the bottom, it says: "The top authority of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina is the Serb Assembly ..." And so on and so forth. Do you remember that you were elected by the Main Board, although I supported another candidate who was in competition with you, and that that was honoured?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite correct, and that's what I told the investigators several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom, I am complaining a bit about our people. I am saying Alija Izetbegovic -- next page in Serbian too: "Alija Izetbegovic never crossed my mind. He is unimportant. It really has to do with our people who are not behaving in terms of loyalty or the policy we have charted. You cannot chop Bosnia-Herzegovina in fragments. You must transform Bosnia-Herzegovina. America came to pay their respects to us. Zimmerman came and said, 'You can't chop up Bosnia-Herzegovina,' and now Brdjo wants me to chop it. No way, you must point out that it's going to remain within its present borders, but you must transform it in such a way that it does not break down. Make it flexible, make it a republic consisting of three sovereign peoples. In this, we found allies in the Croats ..." And so on and so forth. Do you remember that we accepted that Bosnia should leave Yugoslavia with our consent on the condition that it is transformed within, that it is good enough for all three constituent peoples?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember. It was quite clear that that was our policy, that Bosnia-Herzegovina is our state as well, but that there should be an equality of rights or, rather, to avoid a situation in which the Muslim people out-vote the other two peoples.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 22 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Around the middle, in Serbian it says - these are my words: "I do not wish to head this party a single day longer. I think that I have repaid my debt to my people, what I owe to my people. I have no desire whatsoever to remain one more day here. I can hardly wait to return to my profession and my occupation. A better person will be found. It is not a problem. Nobody is irreplaceable." Do you remember that that was my position? I did not put myself up as a candidate for anything; I remained in my profession until the 1st of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire Serb people remember all of this, Mr. President, because the people were wondering why you were not a candidate in the elections in 1990, in the elections for the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because your last name is a well-known one, as opposed to the last name of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic and Koljevic. You would have won a lot more votes of other ethnic groups, not only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to ask whether this document had been admitted in its entirety when it was tendered by the Prosecution. I see, in its entirety. D456, can we have that now briefly. This is the 20th session of the Assembly held on the 14th and 15th of September, 1992, in Bijeljina. Can we now have the Serbian and the English version, please, page 15. Sorry -- yes, it is actually page 15. In Serbian, it's page 17, page 17 in e-court. You can see that it is my words. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to draw your attention to the middle, roughly, the middle of this page in Serbian and also in English: "I must say that it often ..." Et cetera. And this is what it says in Serbian: "I must say that very often some municipal functionaries behave in an illegal way that actually calls for arrests and punishment. We have to point that out as an Assembly, and perhaps we even need to punish it and find a way for the Presidency to take a stand in such matters between two sessions of the Assembly. Namely, we should consider ourselves lucky that there have not been any executions so far, but in the future there will be arrests and punishment. This Assembly, as the legislative body and the body whose duty it is to protect legality, will have to note this and give us authorisation, even if we do not declare a state of war in order to straighten things out in certain municipalities which are of vital importance, to use vigorous measures." Do you agree that rumours and propaganda were destroying us considerably, and I always proceeded from the fact that rumours were correct and I very often criticised people at lower levels basically without any grounds for that? They were being reprimanded; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was criticism levelled at me, too. I remember, specifically, that you said several times that no one allowed looting and that there was looting. There was a fierce struggle being waged for the rule of law, and it was only in the beginning of 1993 that this started functioning in the area of Ilidza. However, that is what war always lent itself to, having the law violated by individuals who bore weapons; rifles, tanks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 53 in Serbian and page 58 in English. In e-court, 53. No, no, it's got to be more than this. It should say "56," five further up in Serbian, and in English, 58. I'm not sure that it's the right page in English either. "Kasagic," where it says "Kasagic." This sentence, this is also my speech: "Tonight, here, we have to say things loud and clear so that I can dismiss and arrest some president of a municipality who is not good. You are clashing against self-management, man. Is self-management a remnant of the previous regime?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And our people encouraged to do whatever they want, should everything be voted on, was that the basis of the socialist system that we had?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self-management was the foundation of the socialist system from 1973 onwards, according to the Associated Labour Act that governed companies and institutions. I was a prominent representative of that kind of work, because I know that law by heart, it was in my bloodstream. I did not know how to operate in a different way. I listened to the grassroots. I listened from the grassroots from around me and from below me. I was more tolerant towards those who were below me than those who were above me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me if you agree that I never got these powers, and if I had wanted to replace you, I would have had to begin a lobbying process among your deputies for them to replace you? In the English, it's page 53. Page 53, please. Is it correct that we never got these powers from the Assembly, and that in order to replace you or any other president of the municipality, I would have done that only by initiating a lobbying process among your deputies for them to replace you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question, but I am waiting. I am simply waiting to see. I don't know when I should begin to speak so that we should not overlap. I, as the president of the Assembly, in order for somebody to be able to replace me, they would have had to convince -- lobby the deputies in the Assembly so that they would replace me at the Assembly and give me a vote of no confidence. There was no other way to replace someone, except when, God forbid, I committed some grave crime, and then the MUP or the military police would have had to arrest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you think of that mechanism when you said that I could have replaced you whenever I wanted?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I practically always asserted that you couldn't replace me whenever you wanted to and that nobody could have replaced me whenever they wanted to, because, simply, I know when I settled in at Ilidza, the MUP was functioning constantly, but when the army began to function, when it established itself and it was maintaining law and order through the MUP and the police, military police, I knew how much of leverage I had among the people; not only in Ilidza, but in Sarajevo as well. Perhaps I made a slip somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that in some testimony, the Prosecution emphasised, based on some interviews, that I could have done that. But was that the only mechanism available to me, had I wanted to replace anyone?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, that is the only legal mechanism.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 30851, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is another telephone conversation on the 2nd of July, 1992, between Dragan Lubura and Nedjeljko Prstojevic. Do I remember correctly that Dragan Lubura was a leader in the Kasindol Local Commune?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dragan Lubura was not a leader in the Kasindol Local Commune, and that's what the problem is, the fact that the representatives -- The Hague representatives -- The Hague investigators do not look at who is the other -- at the other end of the line. This is a person carrying the lowest-ranking civilian procurement job when none of the key people are there. When the president of the commissioner's office, Mr. Zeljaja, is not there, when other people are not there, then he would pick up the phone. If he's not there, then the cleaner would pick up the phone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the following page, please. In English, it's on the first page. Can we stay on the first page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, you're saying that you need to speak with me on the phone, and then you say: "No, somebody blackened our name here."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We don't see the original.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the English, the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you say: "Prominent people from Kasindol told him that," about you. "I had no idea about that, honestly ... one of the best crisis staffs, which does its job the best. They are feeding the hospital and all the people in it, and so on." Again, this is a confirmation of somebody having said something to me against the people in Kasindol and about tarnishing their reputation with me; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the following page in the Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you say, all right, you appointed somebody: "He was no good. He'll be fired. Now, if they insist on appointing someone else, we'll accept that too." And then you go on to say: "But if you want, you can as a local ... I don't think they'll ask the local authority organs anything. "Ilidza municipality will have nothing more to do with the hospital, and you can take upon yourselves the supply of the hospital and everything else." Can we look at the following page in the English, please. Do you agree that again what is being mentioned here is regarding the bad-mouthing and that dispute that Miso is responsible for that? Well, all right, I don't have to read any more. Do we agree? Can we have two pages further in the Serbian and one in the English, I think? I say -- Lubura says: "Well, allegedly Karadzic should also be there, that guy who came to give me certain details told me so." And then you say: "All right. If Karadzic comes, you'll know what needs to be said ..." And so on and so forth. And then that the bottom then, it says they were saying something about the vehicle pool, and I told Karadzic: "They have the papers of the vehicle pool. They collected the people there." And so on and so forth. Is this about care being taken, in the midst of war, that at the hospital and around the hospital, everything is done according to the law?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that's what it was about, to behave according to the law. The Executive Board was not happy with the work of Miso Obradovic, whom it appointed. They wanted to replace him. He complained to the Health Ministry, Mr. Kalinic, and then there was some tensions there. This Kasindol Municipal Staff was very good, and I had put myself on their side. And it's clear, if they want to replace him, then they can do that, but then we will no longer be supplying the hospital, because this was a person who was supplying not only the civilian population, but also the hospital, and this is why we were discussing this. And in time, there will be a change -- a legal replacement of this director.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't doubt that you were much more powerful than the Defence Ministry. Thank you. Can we admit this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1223, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 07177. We had that document before. And can we have page 44 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your testimony of the 15th of June, 2005. I'm just going to read this one answer you gave: [In English] "Well, it's perfectly clear. When the minister of national defence was appointed for the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and certain people in the Territorial Defence were designated, our commander of Territorial Defence Staff in Ilidza was immediately linked through this hierarchy with them, and he had all the necessary consultations and instructions from the people from that ministry. However, if you allow me one more thing, from that date, the 16th of April, until the 19th of May, when the Army of Republika Srpska was created, for the most part, in the area of Ilidza municipality, our staff of Territorial Defence organised our defence on its own initiative, with the verbal support and minimal, almost symbolic logistical support from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska." [Interpretation] Was this also the reason why you felt left to your own devices, and you felt that you had to deal with it yourself, and that there was no key support from the central organs?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely that. It's correct that the Ministry of Defence, which had just been formed, and we know the number of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was unable to provide any kind of assistance. And I am stating now that in this period until the Army of Republika Srpska was formed, all of our defence exclusively rested on the TO Staff, and me, as the commander of the Crisis Staff, and the people down. All assistance could have boiled down to perhaps if they could have checked something on the telephone. There was no other help.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter -- actually, it's the same number, but it's page 96 now. After that, we'll look at 97. Actually, we were supposed to have moved to page 45 to see this last sentence. If this is 96, can we look at line 23. It's right at the bottom. 96 in the e-court. Actually, this is not the page we're looking at. It's the same time document, 07177, page 96, transcript pages 14595. The following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question here is -- I'm going to be reading in English: [In English] "Why did you understand that Mr. Radovanovic had been sent to Ilidza? For what purpose? "A. Well, I never quite understood why the municipalities in the area of Serbian Sarajevo were given commissioners when they had well-established local governments, municipal governments, and other bodies, but those people simply came, told us that they had been appointed, that they were superior to us, that they were going to follow the work of local governments in the municipalities, the work of the MUP, the police and the army, the entire structure functioning in the area of a municipality. And I think -- in fact, I don't think, I know, that the last commissioner for us told us loud and clear that he would inform the leadership in Pale that the Executive Board and the local authorities were operating properly and that there was no need for his presence here. I can't remember the name of the man now. And that's what happened. He informed Pale, and then he left. And later followed the decision of Republika Srpska voiding the decision to establish war commissioners." [Interpretation] Do you agree that it wasn't the case that the power was preserved in all the municipalities, and that municipal assemblies could convene in all of the municipalities, and that it wasn't everywhere like this, and that in some municipalities there was some people who were quite inept at carrying out responsible duties?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. But this man, this second commissioner whom I couldn't remember at the time, is people's deputy Mr. Jovo Mijatovic, and I have here in front of me documents whereby the investigators have evidence that the Assembly introduced commissioners' offices in some municipalities. The National Assembly of Republika Srpska introduced them and later abolished that. I have a notebook in front of me here that says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that with the roads being cut, and the telephones, telefaxes, other communications were compromised to a large extent, and that was also one of the reasons why the central leadership didn't know what was going on, the government didn't know what was going on in the municipalities, and for that reason they wanted to have the presence of these commissioners?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I completely agree, because it's absolutely correct that one didn't know where the seat of the government was, where certain republican functionaries were based, and this kept changing. You would have that they were in one building, and then later in another, and then again another. It was difficult to communicate by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Prstojevic, could you tell us the time-frame when the Pale voided [Realtime transcript read in error "avoided"] the appointment of such war commissioners? I said "voided," not "avoided."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The National Assembly abolished war commissions offices in the decision dated the 18th of December, 1992. Let me check this once again. On the 17th of December, 1992, the war commissioners' offices were abolished. But shortly thereafter, because of the peculiar situation of Ilidza, which was, in territorial terms, divided into three pieces - there was territory controlled by us, then by Muslims, then by us - on the 16th of January, 1993, we, on our own initiative, established a war commission. And in making that decision, I did not consult anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will these two excerpts from testimony be admitted or is it sufficient to have them on the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would add them to the existing Exhibit D1221, four pages, transcript 14542 to 14543, and 14595 to 14596.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Can we have P1487.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am fully aware, Mr. Prstojevic, that it entirely depends on me, whether I will elicit a yes-or-no answer from you, but since we don't have time, I'll try to do just that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P1487, General Mladic's diary, and can we have page 143 in Serbian, and I mean the typed version, and 144 in English. Page 143 in Serbian, the typed version, and 144 in English. We need page 144 in English. We still don't have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say: "We haven't done many things, we haven't constituted a state, not all the verticals are functioning. The state is run by a few men. We did not secure the army. Politics - stop, go - is disastrous for us." You mean the army politics, is that right, there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is some sort of meeting which took place with General Mladic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will get to the date later. Can we now have the next page in both version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 7th of November, 1994. Still, the vertical structures are not well functioning. This seems to be your opinion, and not everyone seems to agree. So can we have 44 in Serbian and 45 in English in e-court. The transcript says: "It seems that others do not agree on this." But based on your participation in the meeting, there was agreement on this issue; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose the transcript reflects a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see about Mr. Radic. Is he the president of the Ilijas municipality and people's deputy, or was he no longer president at the time? I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Trifko Radic was a peoples' deputy from Ilijas, a man held in high repute. I think he had a law degree and worked in the Kosevo Hospital. The president of the Ilijas municipality was Mr. Ratko Hadzic, and the two of them did a great deal for the municipality of Ilijas and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Radic's assessment is that there was general chaos and lack of discipline: "Unless a state of war is declared, I will take up weapons and will never set my foot back in the Assembly. When one individual is wounded, 16 carry him away and abandon the lines." So evidently the notes only reflect the gist of what was said, but do they reflect what Deputy Radic stated at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at the correct English page, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In English, it should be page 145 in e-court. Now we have it. Can we now have 65 ter 10930. It's a meeting of the SDS Town Board, dated the 18th of April, 1991. I do believe that Mr. Radic is among those present, too. But I'm afraid we don't have a translation, so I'll just read out one excerpt from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the minutes from the Town Board meeting, dated the 18th of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under item 6, it reads: "When it comes to the appointment of the Council of the SDS Town Board of Sarajevo, Jovo Jovanovic told those present that the councils would be auxiliary bodies of the Town Board, comprising people with the greatest expertise, education and capabilities proposed by municipal boards." Does this not show that it is the municipal boards who have the authority to put forth candidates for these bodies, rather than have the higher structures interfere in this?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I did say that I was a member of the SDS Town Board.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it marked for identification, and we'll have it translated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1224, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 00948. This is the wrong number. Can we have 16767. We have a translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statutory decision passed by your Ilidza Board in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it read, in the second line from the top: "The presidential shall be held answerable for his activity by the Assembly and the Municipal Board"? Is this how the understood the chain of authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I explained to the investigators that we passed this statutory decision at my express request. Other municipal boards did not have this, but the League of Communists had statutory decisions governing the basic structures of the League of Communists. Guided by that principle, I wanted to organise the work of the Ilidza SDS Municipal Board along these lines. And later on, I came across difficulties simply because I wanted to act in accordance with the law, and this is in accordance with the statute of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1225, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 30862.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your telephone conversation with Jovo Bozic. A female person says: "Yes, hello." "Serbian municipality of Ilidza, President Prstojevic needs to talk to President Bozic." Let me ask you, if General Gvero [Realtime transcript read in error "Jovo Bozic"] called someone, and we don't know who, and if he addressed him as president, how many presidents did we have and how many individuals could he have addressed in this manner?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he could have addressed, as president, all those who were presidents of municipalities. And let me tell you that all the mass media outlets, including radio and television, addressed me as president, as they did you, president of the republic. We had to correct them. In some cases, it wasn't corrected. In some, it was only after or toward the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Any news, anything new to report," Jovo Bozic asks you. And you say somewhere in the middle: "Well, nothing special, to tell you the truth. When it comes to help in this Sarajevo area, there's nothing new to report. We are neither assisted by the higher-up political levels or by the government, nobody. What's more, it was the Sarajevo region that has given more to them than they to us." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 5 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can take a look at line 22 of the previous page, which is on the monitor. Did you ask the witness if Jovo Bozic called someone, or you refer to someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant General Gvero or anyone. I said if we heard anybody address somebody else as president, whereas Jovo Bozic was the person who was in this telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just wanted to check the accuracy of the transcript. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Jovo says: "No way, we have no flats." And you say: "No, they don't have any flats at their disposal, but we should try and find a weekend cottage or something of the sort." And then he tells you: "Please take it upon yourself." And then you go on to say: "You know where the problem lies. I have -- it's very busy here with me in the town." And he says: "I know ... there's a great deal of wheeler-dealers who are taking away flats ..." Et cetera. Can we have the next page in Serbian, please. And he says: "There is a lot less of that at my end, and yet I can't put a stop to it. But please see what you can do." So was it not the case that in Ilidza, the ratio was one local inhabitant to a refugee? Was it a problem to find accommodation for all these refugees?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a big problem, and I have documentation with me here. As early as the 17th of April of 1999, we were discussing the possible accommodation for refugees in Ilidza. We have memos from the Rakovica Local Commune which is on the border with Kiseljak. We also have a memo from a brigade to that effect. The population in the area under our control rose from 20.000 to 45.000, and if we factor in some of the Serbs who were there who had also fled from elsewhere, there were more refugees there than locals. And that's true for Eastern Ilidza as it is for Republika Srpska. And as for the Croats, I said that more than 85 per cent of the Croats stayed with us. They didn't move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This conversation revolved around possibilities of putting up these refugees in weekend cottages, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the periphery of the municipality, including Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1226, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have 65 ter 30863.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your telephone conversation also with the president of the municipality of Rajlovac, Jovo Bozic. And it says down here: "The municipality of Rajlovac." "The president wishes to speak to you." And could we have the second page now. In English, yes, it's the lower part here. Jovo Bozic says: "Is there anything new going on, any news?" And he says: "Nothing special." "Well, do you know anything about this Assembly tomorrow in Banja Luka?" And he says: "I don't know. And you say: "You are invited to the Assembly." Ah, yes, it is the next page in English: "You have been invited to the Assembly in Banja Luka. Well, presidents of SDS municipal boards, tonight ..." And so on. And he sa s: "Yes." And you say: "To tell you the truth, I have decided that I'm not going to Banja Luka." Did you go to Banja Luka then?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I went. I did go once. If I said that I decided I wouldn't go, something could have changed, Jovo Bozic could have persuaded me to go. However, I was there once, and not at that Assembly all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were cases when you did not attend, and nothing bad happened to you because you did not attend?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, nobody would have even asked why I hadn't come.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. I think you can keep the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So some Seso gets into the picture, and Seso says: "If we could meet up to analyse this, about four or five municipalities, Adzic, Bozic, and Andzic from Ilijas." And you say: "You can -- you take that schedule one-on-one meeting somewhere and we will come." Were these meetings a necessary form of work, since there wasn't good communication with the government and the central authorities?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, absolutely, it was necessary, and we had a great many meetings at lower level. This Seso is Svetozar Stanic, who then held the post of the president of the municipality of Vogosca. It was only later that Rajko Koprivica would take over.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1227, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have for a moment, please, P1105. This is a session of the People's Assembly held on the 23rd and 24th of November, 1992. Could we have page 102 in English in e-court, and the Serbian page is ERN 0214-9731. It seems to be page 100 in e-court, the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The chairman is most probably the speaker of the Assembly, Krajisnik. And down here, towards the middle, it says: "Djuric complaining because he is not aware of what the commissioners are doing. I therefore would ask, but I don't know. I don't think they are right. Perhaps they are. I would therefore ask these commissioners. Let me explain only briefly. The function of the commissioners was to ..." Well: "... and most of them were deputies and who went on behalf of the state to places where authority does not function. Try to help resolve some problems so that the authorities could be established." Do you agree that this was their purpose?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. And they were objective, in practical terms, and they helped us in allowing the rule of law to prevail.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 01611.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that those who passed laws know those laws the best; that is to say, members of Parliament?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, we see a certificate confirming that Jovo Mijatovic was appointed a member of Parliament, and instead of the president of the Presidency, it was Krajisnik who initialled this. This is just a certificate stating that the Presidency had appointed him. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do agree, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1228, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 20647.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a decision of the National Assembly. It was signed by President Krajisnik; the speaker of the National Assembly, that is. It is dated the 17th of November, 1992. And Article 1 says: "The decision on the formation of war commissions in municipalities during an imminent threat of war or state of war ceases to be valid." "On the day this decision enters into force, the war commission shall cease to function." And then: "This decision shall enter into force on the day it is issued and shall be published in the 'Official Gazette' ..." Is that what you said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 1656. Part of my question is missing in the transcript. The Assembly passed this, and the Assembly declared it null and void.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you confirmed that?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I confirmed it a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a document of the Serb municipality of Ilidza, dated the 16th of January. I think that you mentioned it a few moments ago. It is an order on the establishment of war presidencies -- of a war presidency. Can you confirm that it is not people by name who are appointed to these war presidencies, but in terms of the office they hold; the president of the Municipal Assembly, the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, secretary of the Municipal Assembly, president of the Municipal Executive Board, brigade commanders on the territory of Ilidza Serb municipality, Ilidza police station commander, Rade Ristic, Vojkovici war commissioner? So it is not that they are appointed there as individual people, but in terms of the office they hold?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite true, it has to do with the offices they hold. This Rade Ristic was pointed out in particular because he pertains to the eastern part, and that will be the same thing there. He will replace me there. It's the same people who are going to be there, the commanders of brigades, et cetera, because Ilidza has three brigades and two battalions and another brigade, then three police stations, plus the border police station and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Article 6 says what the tasks are of the War Presidency: "... to co-ordinate the functions of government (the army, police stations, economic facilities and government organs) for the sake of defending the territory, maintaining and establishing civilian authority, and organising all other parts of life and work on their territory. "They will receive certain instructions from republic government organs and provide necessary information with the aim of ensuring conditions for the work of military organs and units and the police stations for the defence of the Serb people. "They will create conditions and enable the work of charity and humanitarian organisations, i.e., the unhindered transport of humanitarian aid convoys, refugees, prisoners of war and the like." Article 7 says that the War Presidency decisions have to be verified by the Assembly by a majority of votes. Is that customary in our system? Is this customary to have this kind of concentration of power when decisions have to be made urgently, and they have to be subjected to verification in the Assembly once the Assembly can meet?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely. As I said a moment ago, Ilidza was split into three parts. And for the sake of functionality in a situation of war, war was being waged every day, every day people were losing their lives and there was fighting going on, so as soon as the Assembly would meet, they would verify the decisions reached or they would say, No, that's not right and I'm not going to vote for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the members of the Assembly, Municipal Assembly, were also in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, you don't know about this, but the investigators know full well that I closed the municipality a countless number of times, and all the officials went to the trenches to fight. The investigators know that I fought as an infantryman together with Assembly officials for six days. They know that we regularly held the defence line towards Sokolovic Kolonija, several days during the week and for several hours. For example, the soldiers would go home for 15 minutes to take a bath, to have some lunch, and that was it. We were not just rocking in our armchairs. Everyone had to be there on the front-line and fight. Ljubo Bosiljcic was in the Territorial Defence Staff, and he was in charge of logistics. No one was exempt from these defence duties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1230, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have D1164 briefly. This is a document that was exhibited. It is a UN document dated the 15th of September, 1994. Can I have page 4 of this document. I am going to read this now, although I know that you can understand the English, read it in English: [In English] "Movement of people. "The office of ICRC in Hrasnica reported that last Sunday the BH police stopped 100 people, Serbs residing in Hrasnica, from crossing through Mount Igman to Serb-controlled areas. "ICRC employees, who witnessed the return, have been denied to interview these people who, after interrogations at the police station, returned home. "ICRC believes that some of them may have become homeless due to the fact that their apartments were immediately occupied by others. There are some indications that BH authorities may offer an exchange for Muslim residents in Ilidza."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, this report of the United Nations refers to the possibility of this promise made to the Serbs, that they could leave, and as soon as they would leave their apartments, somebody would occupy their apartments, and then they would not actually be allowed to leave. Was that the practice that prevailed?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of this case. Actually, from the 28th of April, 1992, there were a bit over 300 Serbs who were left in Hrasnica, and they were hostages. They were not allowed to leave. However, before this date, somebody from the Muslim authorities had promised the Serbs transport to Kiseljak, and had taken money from them for that, and people know how much money it was. They were supposed to provide buses and everything else that was needed. However, when they were taken to Igman, then this happened, what the UN is saying here. Now, when they were returned to Hrasnica, then these Serbs - I mean there were women there, children, and some able-bodied men - they were spat at, mistreated. Various objects were thrown at them by the Muslim population there, in the presence of the authorities and those who had organised their departure. This is pure manipulation. Secondly, it is incorrect that we have Muslims in Ilidza for exchanges, because we had freedom of movement. However, there was no freedom of movement only for Serbs who were of military age. They could only desert, but everybody else was allowed to go wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 1994, in Ilidza, there were still Muslims living there who hadn't wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. President. I believe that as a physician, you know Dr. Vlado Mehmetbasic [phoen]. Throughout the war, he was with us. His villa, his house, is in this alley -- this big street, rather, where the Command of the Ilidza Brigade was 150 metres away.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This has already been admitted, so let's move on. 65 ter 07177, please. That's the document that we already had. And then in e-court, it is page 127, 127.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read out this answer of yours in English: [In English] "The Muslims were not -- in Ilidza were not being expelled in an organised fashion, and this can be proved for the entire -- for this entire area. It was in the areas that were -- combat activities were being conducted that Muslims were driven out. In 1992, there were numerous Muslim units in the area, and under such circumstances even thousands of households would actually move out, but both on the Muslim and Serb side. Throughout the war, many homes were left abandoned, those that were abutting the line of contact, the line of confrontation as the people were leaving the area. However, the Muslim and Croat population were allowed to go wherever they wanted to go if they wanted to. Initially, they were allowed to go wherever they wanted to go, and then subsequently they were allowed to go to those municipalities where there were no combat activities under Croat control because the front-line was held so strictly that civilians could cross these areas only through organised exchanges." [Interpretation] Does this correctly reflect the circumstances and the manner in which the civilians could have avoided the areas in which they did not want to stay?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, Mr. President, during my interview in 2003, I was working in a company from 7.00, and sometimes I was interviewed for over 19 hours. I was unprepared and often I was tired, and I told the investigators on a number of occasions, I'm tired, but I will answer that question. And they abused that. I wasn't precise here, but also the interpreter -- I have about 20 objections to the translation from 2003, the mildest one of which would be I didn't say that. The investigator would then give a break, and then afterward that they would say, You said so and so. There are two cases like that. Here, I could not have said that the Muslims were expelled somewhere. What is the gist? The areas where there is fighting is an urban area, it's part of the town. The population was fleeing on its own, both Serbs and Muslims and Croats. Everybody was escaping because the fighting had started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was saying in 2003, in essence, is correct, but it's not precise enough. The most clear formulation would be nobody ever moved out the population from Ilidza during wartime in an organised manner, or from any other area. Because of combat, the population from all three ethnic groups was fleeing on its own. We can give examples. Let's say the priest from the monastery in Nedzarici is somebody who was an eye-witness of all of these events. I will mention that as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that Catholic monastery was preserved on our side. The whole time, you had preserved the monastery and returned the library to them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 154 in the same document in the e-court. This is the testimony of the 16th of June, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 1 here, it states -- 154 in e-court, and the page is 14659. So it's the following page, please. You state: [In English] "We did not expel any Muslims in an organised fashion from Ilidza, and we did not undertake anything else against the Muslim population." [Interpretation] And the question: [In English] "Isn't it the case that repressive measures were taken against Muslims, which resulted in them increasingly fleeing from the territory? "A. I don't know if any repressive measures have been taken, but whoever was in a minority in a given area would not have been safe. And the population moved en masse. No matter what population, if they were not in a majority, they would tend to move to those areas where they were." [Interpretation] Is this also your answer that you can confirm again today?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally, this applied, and I confirmed that. But Ilidza -- the Serbs from Ilidza, the inhabitants there, were extremely tolerant in comparison to refugee Serbs, who were disappointed, had suffered casualties and were like this or like that, and they could have created situations like that. I stand by what I said. I think in 2005, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we add these pages, too, to the document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we need the previous page as well in order to understand the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. And in order to understand the context, Your Honour, with respect to the pages -- now referring back to the first reference that begins at 14631, that discussion continues through to the beginning of 14638, so I think we should include those. And as to 1465 -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean eight pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. And as for the discussion that begins at 14659, that continues on to the next page, 14660, and I will check to see if the underlying document, which is identified at page 14658 - so maybe we should start there - is in evidence. And I think for context, it would need to be. So for that section, it would be 14658 through 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough in relation to the second part. Are you happy to admit eight pages, Mr. Karadzic, in relation to the first part?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have no objection if Mr. Prstojevic would confirm that these are faithfully convey stance. Otherwise, we would have a problem. Perhaps, in the questioning, Mr. Tieger could ask if those pages are okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see the page 127 first, transcript page 14631. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have to disagree with the accused's suggestion, Your Honour. He raised this point. This is testimony in court, transcribed and recorded. These additional pages are in the precise same context the accused tendered them. There is no need for the expedient of going through it with the witness, who said those words in court, and they can be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not correct, man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prstojevic, it's not for you to interfere at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think page 127 speaks for itself. And if necessary, you can deal with the remainder of the pages referred to during re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll have a limited time in -- I'll bow to the Court's will, of course, but I think that is a clear continuation, and I think it should be included, particularly since this occurred in open court, as part of the questioning which the accused seeks to tender.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this moment, we'll admit just one page, 14631, and it's entirely up to you, Mr. Tieger, to raise the remainder of the pages referred to. So we'll add these four pages to Exhibit D1221. And I note the time. It's time to take a break. As I indicated to you, Mr. Karadzic, I would expect you to conclude your cross-examination in the next session. Half an hour. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, Mr. Tieger was kind enough to tell us that he would need at least those 45 minutes, and perhaps a whole hour, so if the Trial Chamber wouldn't have many questions, I would ask to have some half an hour from that session, to use this opportunity that the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that we allowed you originally 10 hours, that request is admitted. You'll have half an hour in the next session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can we have 65 ter 223 -- 22231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems to be another technical difficulty in relation to the French translation. We are not getting any. Shall we try again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If the Court Deputy could see to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we now have French translation? I hope the matter has been resolved. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Lattanzi has kindly agreed to follow in English in the meantime. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 22231. This is your statement of the 6th of May, 2005, just a small excerpt. E-court page 49 in English, and in the B/C/S, 48. 98 in Serbian. The English is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am going to read it in English. The question is: [In English] "What does the term 'ethnic cleansing' mean?" Prstojevic: "I simply do not know, because we did not use that term in our terminology during the war. Simply because of security, for example, Sarajevo had 176.000 Serbs. All the Serbs that were not under the control of Serbs, which means that they were under control of Muslims or Croats, they wanted to leave those territories, and for them, that was saving their lives." [Interpretation] Do you agree, Mr. Prstojevic, that this was a temporary relocation of the population in order to save their lives, and it was regulated by at least four international agreements with the other two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that in front of me, and I'm trying to process it in detail. As far as international conventions are concerned, I'm aware of only one thing. The combat area, where it was not safe for the population, where there was destruction of buildings, it's possible or it's permissible to move out the population. I stand by what I said in 2005. As for Ilidza, and I state this, never carried out any organised relocation of the population anywhere, because that would imply organising buses, providing transport for the people, and so on and so forth. However, as for Serbs in Sarajevo, leaving the Muslim territory meant reaching freedom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we add this page? Can we -- actually, this is a different document. This is a statement; it's not testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, only that page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1231, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 14692 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a document here signed by the president of the Municipal Assembly. We will see that at the end. And what is being sought here from the Bosnia-Herzegovina Government is to adopt two decisions, to return Serbs from Serbia and Montenegro and that their property shall be confiscated. I assume that means in case they don't return. But let's look at paragraph 4. From the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, not only the Serb, but Muslim and Croat population have also moved out. Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite correct. Until that fateful day, the 22nd of April, 1992, when that horrendous attack on us took place, more Serbs were killed than Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1232, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of course, this threat of confiscation of Serb property, of deserters, is something that you never actually carried out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, here's what's important: It's very important to differentiate between something that is said from the possibility of actually implementing it. We were not an organ, at the level of the municipality, that could do that, that could actually carry that through. In order to confiscate property, you need to adopt legal regulations at the level of the state. The attempt here was to return military conscripts, Serbs, from Serbia and from Montenegro, and some of our activities in that area were effective to have deserters come back to defend their country and their -- or their land and their houses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 01535. 01535.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your document, dated the 19th of May, 1992, where a decision is issued allowing the departure of the Croats and Muslims from all the areas of the Serb municipality of Ilidza, save for Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica, where such departures are not allowed. Were Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir and Hrasnica under your control or were they under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica, Butmir and Donji Kotorac were under Muslim control throughout the war. Nobody has a shred of any valid proof, the orders of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, or Ilidza, or any other units which would have issued orders to attack. These settlements have a corridor by way of Igman, a way out, and this was the way which some of the Serbs took, as confirmed by UNPROFOR. We were angry because the Serbs were not allowed free movement, and all the discussions ended unsuccessfully. At a later date, we would amend this decision, and it only takes a day or two to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 16774, a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, people who wanted to have free movement, would they approach an authority to be issued with permits to that effect or were permits forced on them?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Mr. President, with a view to prohibiting military conscripts, the Serbs, from leaving Ilidza, we, and I mean first the Crisis Staff and then the MUP, started issuing permits. When the Army of Republika Srpska was set up, only the permits issued by the MUP and the VRS would be valid, and they applied solely to conscripts. In this particular instance, it has to do with permits for Serbs, military conscripts, because, otherwise, the MUP or the VRS would not -- or the TO, that is, would not allow them to leave, and only those [Realtime transcript read in error "Serbs"] holding permits could be allowed passage at check-points. Secondly, all the remaining population who were not military conscripts were not issued permits. This is also applicable to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here that only the Serbs could pass through check-points with these passes. That's what the transcript says. Can we clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does everyone who holds such a pass, and who has a wartime assignment either as a work obligation or at the front, be it Serb or Muslim, have the right to pass -- go through the check-point, and those who didn't have them wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Whoever had the pass was guaranteed passage. Even here, with me in The Hague, I have a pass for -- issued for a Muslim. Such passes were issued by my own associates, and I and they can testify to the fact that these passes were received also to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have 65 ter 30784.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telephone conversation which took place on the 21st of May, 1992, between you and -- or, rather, between Unkovic and Gagovic and then between you and General Mladic. Can we have page 2, please. Rather than read everything, let me just summarise this. You greet Mladic, and then Mladic says: "Listen, the convoy set out ..." And he's telling someone to lower the volume of something: "A convoy is set out from the barracks. They turned over the food stuffs ..." And please look at what he says next. Tolimir: "And then they have a warrant officer second class on board without [indiscernible]." And then he says: "Tolimir went there. Their convoy should be prepared immediately, and it should be the same as it was when it came here. It should go straight to Kobiljaca. You will be escorted, and you will not hold it up."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Karadzic repeat his question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat your question, please, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this telephone conversation with Mladic mean that a convoy carrying food set out, and that it was accompanied by a warrant officer of armija -- that's to say of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who had an ulcer perforation, and that it was supposed to go straight to Kobiljaca? Would it cross over to the BH Army territory upon reaching Kobiljaca?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation needs to be explained in greater detail. It does mean precisely that, but it has to do with a convoy of children from Sarajevo and conscripts from Sarajevo. The convoy is some eight kilometres' long. This activity was run by the Ministry of Health. The convoy reached eight kilometres into our territory, and there were problems on the Muslim side because they wanted to include among those in the convoy also the defenders of Sarajevo. However, since there had been a massacre committed in Pofalici earlier on, the Serbs would approach the convoy, asking that some 317 civilians, Serbs who were killed on that occasion, and 70 who were taken prisoner. I have very precise information about this. What you stated in your question is true, but let me say this: In relation to this particular date, the 19th, there is a forgery, a faked decision of the Crisis Staff, which I have been in possession of since 2000, but I knew that it wasn't genuine, it wasn't ours. And this was also confirmed by an official of the American Embassy. And last winter, as I was looking at the documentation, I observed that the stamp wasn't ours at all, and, of all things, the stamp contains a swastika. And I compared it to our stamp which I wanted to show to Dusko, the individual who had been given this document to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, let's go on. It says here that Mladic would explain to people from Pofalici and is asking you not to stall the matter, as the Muslims have been. Can we have the next page. The English page is all right. You say: "We have always been fair." And Mladic is kindly asking you: "I'm not saying that you haven't been fair, but please tell these families. Let them take some water ..." Et cetera. And you say: "Fine, it will be done." So you were told that the convoy should be given food and water and that Mladic would take upon himself to explain this to the people of Pofalici. Do you know that Mladic's house in Pofalici was burned that day? Did you know that he had a house there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely true, his house was torched. And this convoy would be taken care of by our border police. I have an exact annotation in my diary as to the measures we took to secure the convoy; for instance, to have a police officer 100 metres -- police officers 100 metres apart, to have care taken of women with infants, if any, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 30788.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Rather than read the whole document, let me tell you that you're talking to Colonel Gagovic on the 21st of May yet again, and he asked you if anybody was bothering you. You complained that you had too many people in your charge, and I suppose it refers to refugees. Can we have the next page. Did you mean refugees when you said that you had too many people there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant refugees as well, but we had some five to six conversations about this particular convoy. The Muslim leadership launched a widespread offensive in Sarajevo and then charged us with this particular convoy and waited to see what would happen with the people who had had members of their families killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here that you were worried about Alija because he did not take care of his people: "The only thing he's doing is bad-mouthing me in the media." The answer you gave was not complete. You said the Muslims sent a convoy, and you said that they placed 200 of some others, expecting that the families of those killed - I suppose in Pofalici - would make a problem out of it. What did you mean, exactly?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I meant: The convoy held a large number of military conscripts, more than 200, I suppose, because the column was more than eight kilometres' long, so you'll understand that if somebody's family was killed the day before, and there were many families there whose people were among the 317 who perished there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You can see on this page that you say: "I will have to explain to the people. We were explaining to them somewhat that it was Alija's sin." So you were explaining to the people that it was Alija's fault because of his lack of care; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that he is not showing any interest, it's not the powerless who are to blame, and then you say: "Well, he's manipulating them. He'd like to achieve something with the public by doing that, but we'll see. Maybe things will resolve themselves somehow today." And you're referring to the convoy, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page. And we can keep the English. The relevant part is at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Gagovic is telling you this: "These Muslims are fleeing Dobrinja head over heals." "Is that so?" "I ordered the press centre to make it known that we will allow only entire families of Muslims to leave Dobrinja ..." So: "... husbands, wives, children." "But only entire families. We will not allow women and children to leave alone, leaving the others behind." Therefore, Gagovic is telling you that he will allow civilians to leave, but he also wants men to leave, rather than men getting civilians out of their way and staying behind and fighting there?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, we had the Red Cross and their Crescent meeting to agree on some issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1236, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 31629.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your conversation with one Ekanovic on the 14th of July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Of the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're reading from the fifth or sixth line from the top: "Let them find a solution for that." And you say that you are now in the same sort of situation where you were on the 4th and 5th of April, and: "... I have that situation here now. It's incredible." So you're confirming that you haven't progressed, but you haven't regressed either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you say here is: "The question is -- the question is one of survival."
