And then you're saying: "The situation seems to have no way out, and when things do not start right, we have to narrow things down. Everything will go to the devil. There is no space, you can barely breathe." What is meant here; the fact that the front-lines have practically reached the houses themselves, that they have really pushed you all the way to your houses?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. We had to be like a hedgehog in order to defend ourselves. Later on, we managed to stretch out. I don't know who it is I'm talking to here. I'm assuming that I'm talking to Mr. Kezunovic, who is going to Pale. But my primary concern here has to do with the surrender of the airport to UNPROFOR, which is cutting Ilidza off, what we were talking about the other day. Instead of being able to go to the eastern part and to go home within 15 days [as interpreted], and instead of getting the wounded to where they're supposed to be taken, one has to travel for three hours, rather than fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1237, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 30803, can we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your conversation with General Mladic on the 24th of May. You see in the lower half, Mladic is asking you whether you have buses there from Pofalici, with aid for Sarajevo. And you say that you have prepared everything that you have, and you say that there has been a misunderstanding somewhere. And he's saying: "What?" And you say: "Caritas buses practically entered much earlier. They entered before the convoy ..." And you say: "Where did they enter?" And you say: "In Sarajevo and Ilidza." Is Caritas a Catholic humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you would regularly let them enter Sarajevo through Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. President. As for us in Ilidza, Caritas, all the other humanitarian convoys - I have five or six convoys jotted down here, the ones we let through before the 19th of May - UNPROFOR also had no problems with us. Also, UNPROFOR aircraft flying low. I don't know whether anybody had any problem with us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mladic is asking who is controlling Stup, and you say that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find this on either page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Mladic is saying: "Who is controlling Stup?" And you say: "We allowed a Croatian municipality to be established in Stup and to have control half-half." And further down, Mladic says that food was unloaded near Caritas and that that food should be given to them, that it should go to them. And then you say: "It doesn't cost anything. It means we'll have to call the MUP. All right, we'll get it done." And he said: "You arrange this with our MUP. Commander Milenko is here as well ..." And so on. And towards the bottom, it says: "Agreed." And now: "This is a matter of convention. When can I see you?" Et cetera. First of all, Mladic doesn't know who has Stup under their control on the 24th of May, which speaks of the lack of communication involved. And, secondly, Mladic is saying something, and you are agreeing; namely, that the Caritas food be allowed to get through and that they should be allowed to receive it?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, they were let through. But there were some problems there as well, and it was the border police, our border police, that took care of this; not the regular police, the border police. These are two different police forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 30808.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telephone conversation on the 26th of May between the minister of justice and Tomo Kovac, your boss, the chief of police in Ilidza, and they are exchanging conventional greetings here. And now can we have the second page. Kovac is complaining here, saying that there are some people who are driving Muslims out. And Mandic is asking for criminal reports to be filed, for detention to be set. And Kovac says: "Muslims cannot be expelled from here, from Ilidza." And the one-but-last says: "It's not only a question of the president. He cannot deal with them either. There has to be agreement from above." And so on. Is that what you said, that refugees from Central Bosnia were intolerant of your local Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely, precisely. Mr. Kovac is saying here that we in Ilidza cannot manage all of this by ourselves, and he is asking for someone to be sent in, some armed formation from the top, a special police unit or a special MUP unit, to help us, because Ilidza is already chock-a-block full of refugees, people have nowhere to live. Various places, like Nedzarici, although they are under our control, there are no Serbs living there, but there is the population of 2.000 to 3.000, and they only go in during the night. No one wants to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about what Mandic says previously: "Let us see about this president of the Crisis Staff." And Tomo Kovac is saying: "It's not only a question of the president. He cannot deal with them either." This has to do with the president of the Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not the Crisis Staff that is number one here. It is the civilian police that is in charge here, where Mr. Kovac is in charge, and it is the police of the Army of Republika Srpska that is in charge, the Command of the Ilidza Brigade, because the conversation pertains to its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Their assessment was that you could not manage either without additional police forces, that you cannot deal with all these offences and violations?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on, this is what they're saying: A clear message should be sent to Ilidza and the armed forces. And then Kovac says: "No one made a decision to move the Muslims out." And this entire conversation, as you can see for yourself, says that there's this clash between the police and the territorials. And then Mandic says: "It has to be the army. The Territorial Defence is no more, it has been dissolved." And so on. And then it says: "Look, they are the army now, but they are now a bit better." And so on: "Only when Karadzic signs --" No, this is what Mandic is saying: "Nothing else." Only Mladic can reach such a decision; nobody else. Does this correspond to the situation on the 26th of May, 1995, that the Territorial Defence is being transformed into the army and that Ilidza needs additional forces in order to maintain law and order?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what it means. On the 20th of May, the Ilidza Brigade was established. This is what I wish to add here: We cannot manage this on our own. Secondly, if somebody is speaking of the president of the Crisis Staff, while I have already started functioning as the president of the municipality as of the 20th, and I'm keeping both offices in my hands, I do not have any other instrument in my hand but the civilian police. That is not under me, and also the army is not under me either, so my powers are declarative.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 1553, please. No, this isn't it. 65 ter 1553. Yes, now we have it. This is a bulletin of daily events for the 2nd and 3rd of June, 1992. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Prstojevic that what is being described here are break-ins and assaults against Serb families, Cetic, Markan Dugonjic, and then: "We were informed that members of the Green Berets were moving from the direction ..." And so on and so forth. Doesn't this first part show that the Serbs are equally unsafe in all that chaos, just like the Muslims? Actually, on that particular day, it was the Serbs that suffered more than the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1240, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have P1110.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation of yours taking place on the 2nd of June. You are talking to Mr. Mandic, minister of justice, the same day that that bulletin of daily events pertained to. Can we have the next page, please. Momcilo Mandic is saying: "It came up there to the government and to us that you are giving --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3. It's not right in Serbian: "It has come to our attention and that of the government that you are issuing ultimatums to some Turks, evicting people from certain settlements, and people respond badly to it. They are taking advantage of this, those Muslims in the media ..." And so on. And you say: "Yes." And he's explaining, and this next response is saying: "Well, please, don't do anything like that. First consult Djeric ..." That's the prime minister; right? "... and those people up there. We cannot cleanse either Ilidza or any other place ethnically." That is the position of the government -- at least, that is the position of the government and political leadership, is how we reached the top. In some settlements, you gave them 24 hours to move out, and they -- and so on. You say: "Where did I say that?" And then he's giving an answer. And then you are saying: "I know, but we did not say that, not in public. That's not our policy." Mandic says: "I know. I know what it should be and how we should operate." And you're saying: "Yes, but we did not say that in public anywhere, nor did we write it." And then Mandic is explaining that some Fadil Musanovic, a Muslim, should be appointed a judge. And I don't think I have to read this, anybody can read this. So let's have the next page. You're saying: "With the best of intentions, in view of what the Muslims did as for the blockade in Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija, it's been a month now that no Serbs have left." And Mandic says: "I know. My sister and my father are there." And you're saying: "No one got out of there, although we are allowing them to leave immediately. Let them take 5.000 Muslims from there, and let them allow that many Serbs to leave. We are not in a position to do that. We are not in a position to let someone work. Our misdemeanors court has not received a single report yet, no one has submitted any." And he says: "Well, make Tomo Kovac do that." And so on. Can we have the next page, please, the last page. And it says here: "Please discuss this with your people." Tomo Kovac: "Work on that so the people would be punished, because these criminals and profiteers are extremely active." And Prstojevic says: "That's right." "But, you see, only the other day we received -- actually, we received --" And then further on, you say: "Yes, the 'Official Gazette' number 6. We only received that the day before yesterday." And you're saying: "Only now can we have a legal basis for this, we can start working."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, my first question: Is it correct that there were a lot of rumours that were going around, and propaganda, bad-mouthing, saying that some things that actually never happened did happen?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But this speech demands an analytical approach and explanation, because the Prosecution, for reasons unknown to me, ascribe major significance to this speech, and I don't know why. When you approach it from an analytical aspect, you can see that I immediately told the minister that this was not correct. When I listen, what was said, and I have it in the Serbian on the page that is in front of me, I use the word "reci kaze" [phoen] because I'm surprised, "do tell, say." But then when he told me what it was, I immediately told him, Well, where did I say that? I didn't say that. I simply don't know what the minister was thinking in stating that incorrect thing, the incorrect thing about the MUP and then the incorrect thing about the government, because during those 10 days from the 20th of May up to this day, there were no armed battles, there were none. The Muslims were preparing, regrouping, for the offensive that would be launched on the 8th [Realtime transcript read in error "18th"] of June, so it was quiet. The second thing is at this point in time, Mr. Mandic was sitting in Kula, in the eastern part of Ilidza, where there are five Ilidza local communes. He can see all the Muslim local communes, Sokolovic Kolonija, Butmir, Hrasnica, Donji Kotorac, better than I could, and he couldn't tell me where I said that. So I said, We don't have the instruments. Even if we wanted to, we don't have the instruments in our hands, because the military is independent and the MUP is independent. And that is probably what he thought when he was speaking with Kovac, meaning individuals that were not under control were the ones who were creating the problems. I clearly said our politics is -- it's not our policy to issue ultimatums to remove people, but the investigators were proceeding along their own track, and so on and so forth. And in the end, you can see that he bad-mouthed the MUP, saying that the MUP was stealing, looting, they weren't doing anything, which is quite incorrect. In my testimony from 2003, where I looked at this speech of mine analytically, Mr. Mandic pulled back, and at one point he said, All right, that does not refer to Ilidza. Simply, this is not correct, and nobody can prove that an ultimatum was issued anywhere. They cannot bring one single witness forward, a Muslim witness, to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the transcript, it should say the 8th of June as the start date of the offensive, not the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in the conversation of the 26th of May, you said that Alija Izetbegovic was bad-mouthing you in the media, and do you recall that there was a lot of propaganda and a lot of lies that were published, among other things, about Ilidza too?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, Mr. President, but let me remind you. When we established the crisis -- when the Muslims established their Crisis Staff for Bosnia and Herzegovina in May, and the Croats did that in September 1991, immediately, according to socialist methods, in a strategic way they took the initiative into their own hands and declared the Serbs as the aggressors. We have that in our documents, where it is said, literally, "name the aggressor." And throughout the whole war, it was the propaganda that got to us, because they were lobbying numerous journalists. The most correct were the military analysts. Let me give you an example of Viktor Bezruchenko. In all his testimony to date, I never had any problems with military analysts. We would resolve what's what in five minutes, because they know the situation, whereas investigators don't understand many things. They ascribe importance to them, and they don't have that importance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have D416 for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, let me ask you this, Mr. Prstojevic: You wrote to the government about using abandoned houses and flats, and on the 5th of June, 1992, the government -- the secretary of the government gives you a response; isn't that right? You say -- and says that: "The government finds that citizens whose apartments or houses have been destroyed may obtain only temporary solutions for occupancy of deserted houses or apartments." And they say: "The government will make a proposal for a special regulation ..." Do you remember that problem; that you sent an inquiry to the government as to what to do on this matter, and the government replied with this letter?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and I will add only this: Before this happened, the government will adopt legislation to regulate this particular area. We sealed abandoned apartments on our own initiatives, Serbs, Muslim and Croat apartments. This didn't yield any results, because practically this was a sign that the apartment was free. And then en masse, break-ins occurred, and that's why we were asking the government what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution showed you P1515 in the case. This is a conversation of the 25th of June, 1992, where, in that intercept, the awarding of Muslim apartments to Serbs is referred to. Before that, on the 26th -- actually, we're talking about the 5th of June, and this is admitted. Can we move on. Giving permissions was actually based on this letter by the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was on a temporary basis. These certificates or this permission to move into an apartment was of a temporary nature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 11258, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was also given to Serbs and Croats -- to anyone who lived in Ilidza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is this the decision regulating the allocation of accommodation or flats? Actually, we can move to page 2 immediately. You can see it better on that page. Isn't it correct that an apartment is being -- is this Kata Timotija, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that an apartment is being issued to her for her use, because her house had been damaged in the war, and this is resolved as in the dispositive?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You can see in the preamble that these are -- this is a decision based on the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it's about temporary occupation, isn't it, of the apartment; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1241, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D111 for a minute, please. D111. It's a translation. Can we zoom on it a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This has been signed by me on the 23rd of August, 1993 [as interpreted], so I'm a little bit lagging behind on these matters that have already been regulated by the government. In the introduction, it says: "It has become common for local people to move into empty flats instead of refugees, and they sometimes even retain some kind of 'right' to several flats. "The occurrence of abandoned flats is a wartime issue, and so are refugees. This means that both of these occurrences are of a temporary nature." And then I issue this instruction in what way temporary accommodation can be awarded and to whom. Do you recall these instructions? I think that they were published in the "Official Gazette" and issued to every municipality.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this, and I know about a series of measures requiring urgent action issued by the government. The situation was similar in other municipalities, too. There were scores of thousands of Serbs who had been relocated from other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 16766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, did you say what other municipalities are that you referred to? The interpreters couldn't hear the last words of your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant referred to the Ilidza municipality and the area of combat, the whole area covered by the front-lines. Our population was fleeing as well, so that in our municipality, we had whole settlements where our citizens couldn't live, so we had to dissolve with the housing issues in the depth of the territory, where it was safer. So we had to give solutions to those who came from Central Bosnia, from Sarajevo, and also to those who came to us from our own municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 16776, 65 ter 16776.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document by the Serbian municipality of Ilidza of the 21st of July, and you can see that it says here what all the outstanding issues on the agenda are. It states: "Take all measures to liberate, preserve and surround the territory of Ilidza Serb municipality, and have civil authority in place in the real sense of that word. "Also, all measures are to be taken to preserve the necessary unity of citizens ..." Does this mean regardless of their ethnicity and religious affiliation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then it says: "In order for work and life to function on the territory of Ilidza municipality, the military authorities and the Ilidza Police Station are obliged to execute their tasks and do their work with devotion, fairly and conscientiously." Can we look at the next page, please. Everything is important, but what it says here: "Pay special attention to citizens leaving Ilidza municipality." And then a bit lower, it says: "Strictly take care about all material goods and preventing robbery, loot, and all other forms of crimes in the area of the Ilidza municipality. Therefore, misdemeanor, criminal and other measures must immediately be taken to prevent any abuse or possible crime of any kind." Is this an authentic document, and were these the things that the civilian authorities attempted to do?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an authentic document. I think I have the original even with me here. And I think this is a conclusion from a meeting of myself, as the president of the municipality, and the municipal functionaries. I always tried to get the most responsible people together as a working consultative meeting, where we could agree and establish what to do, then turn that into a written document, into a record of the meeting, and then move to implementation. At the following meeting, we would then go over what things were done and what things were not done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 1418. This is a book of duty transfer at the police. Can we now look at Serbian page 30 and English page 16. The entire document is worth looking at, but we don't have time for that. Can we look at page 30 in the Serbian. In the English, page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it not state here: "Upon the permission of the commander, Andrej Juretic, son of Zdravko, born on 2nd February ...," and so on and so forth, "... was brought in. The same person, with the approval of the commander, was sent to the barracks. At 1130, the Crisis Staff from Kasindol arrested Pero Golijanin from Kasindolska Street. The same person was released after being questioned and with the approval of operative worker Luka Majsorovic [phoen]." And then it goes on: "At 1330 hours, the military police from Kasindol arrested Dusan Matic ..." And: "At 1530 hours, the Crisis Staff from Lukavica arrested Daliborka Delberovic." Are these all Serbs that are being arrested by the police?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bottom four are completely Serbian, and these are males, military conscripts. The first one at the top, I don't know, but it's -- well, the first person could be a Croat. But it's evident that this is a military conscript that is being brought in, and this is a kind of spot check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the basis for this arrest is not ethnicity, but some other kind of action; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's evident that these are military conscripts who are being arrested for the purpose of mobilisation. It's a check of what they're doing. Are they walking around or what?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 26 in the Serbian -- in the English, and page 28 in the Serbian. 48 in the Serbian, actually. That is not 48, I think. It must be 16. Yes, yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is the 1st of July, 1992. This is a description of all the things that happened that day. It states: "The telephone is still not working." And then the entire document, until the end, at least up to the 28th of July, reports from day to day that the telephone line, for example --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The telephone is still not working, so on each page it is noted that the phones are faulty, they're not working. Is it your information as well that your phones were cut off and you had difficulty getting anybody outside of Serbian Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, practically as of the 18th of June, 1992, when fighting took place during the June offensive launched by the Muslims, which lasted 50 days, since the PTT office was close to UNPROFOR in Nedzarici, on the 18th of June the telephone lines of the entire southern area were cut off, Vojkovici, Grlica, Krupac, Kasindol, Kotorac, and parts of Dobrinja, and this would remain the case through to the end of the war, with the exception of the military police and MUP telephone lines, which would eventually be up and running. In the civilian area, we would only have two telephone lines available and one line at a later date in Dobrinja. In other words, around 10.000 inhabitants had no telephone lines that were operational as of the 18th of June, and the situation was the same for the military and the army -- and the MUP, save for the few lines that they had. It was the Muslims who cut off these lines in the PTT switchboard facility in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of this, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1418, 1418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1243, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P2450, P2450. This is a programatic declaration of the Ilidza SDS for the wartime period, and it goes on to say: "In all places and at all times --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't aware of where Mr. Karadzic is quoting from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those -- item 6 in English. Can we have the next page or two pages from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 6, you have it there. Were you able to read it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that document with me. It's clear that this was our position, that we were struggling to have the rule of law. The Prosecutor asked me who the dragon was. Well, we meant that it was the Islamic fundamentalism. Let me tell you that St. George is the patron of Ilidza, is the patron saint of Ilidza, and I have here a document from the Ilidza municipality documents bearing the symbol of St. George killing the dragon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't say "black vultures." You said "the black dragon"?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said, The dragon with black wings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that is the dragon?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is the life of St. George, the Christian saint. And I have here the image of St. George killing the dragon and saving a girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, because I asking you this because it was translated that you said "vultures with black wings," and not "dragon." That's what the translation says.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, translations at times completely twist the meaning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 1662, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was in February, and we now have a document from April. If refugees were returning, was it your duty to guarantee their safety?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely true that we had to ensure the safety of refugees and find accommodation for them. What's more, some of these people were looking to find a job. What I have here with me dating from that period, and specifically the following month, is a report of the Serbian National Security, which details the state of security in Ilidza. There are some 13 bullet points here detailing lack of security, and I'll name only three. Fire was opened at a tank from the municipality and brigade buildings. Our military police clashed with the civilian police. And classic-type murders were committed by a Serb against a Serb, and the authorities of the Croatian Herceg Bosnia issued 150 permissions for people to move into the Ilidza municipality, and we honoured them. I have here a document from General Mladic allowing the passage of 2.000 Croat refugees from Central Bosnia, Vares and Kiseljak, across our territory for the following couple of months. There was some soldiers passing through, as ordered by the Main Staff, complete with their weapons. All of this followed the decision that we issued.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? And can I ask the Trial Chamber if, by their leave, the witness could hand over the documents to the Registry, and perhaps those could, as well, be admitted, the assessment of the State Security of the security situation and the decision by Mladic allowing 2.000 individuals to traverse the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1244, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't have any problem you get the document from the witness via the Victims and Witnesses Section, but it's up to you, whether you tender it or not with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like these two to be admitted, at the very least, and I would like Mr. Prstojevic to hand over to the Registrar all the documents he referred to during his testimony as sources of the facts he related. Could these two documents be assigned a number? I haven't seen them, but they are authentic, without a doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is no basis at this moment to admit any document we haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we now have 65 ter 40200. This is a transcript of an interview with Mr. Krajisnik on TV about the establishment of Republika Srpska. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the middle, the document reads: [In English] "We realised that both Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were disintegrated, and on those ruins, of both Bosnia and Yugoslavia, we were laying foundations for the new country. During those two phases and even afterwards, lots of anarchy appeared, and other things that we did not support appeared as well. And the law tries to implement that/he is probably referring to decisions they made on the establishment of Republika Srpska/as much as possible. "We also established our own army in the second phase, and that represents the shaping of country's foundations. The third phase, which is already behind us, represents enactment of all the laws as the ground work for the functioning of the country. And during that enactment of the laws, we were also dogged by a certain consequences of the disintegration of Yugoslavia and the federal unit of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is, we could not establish absolute regularity of the functioning of authority, even though it was far and away better than in the Croatian or Muslim part. We are now near the end of the third phase, in which we are putting a crone of that, let me just say, the base of a certain country." This interview took place on the 1st of January, 1995. Do you agree that the introduction of a rule of law was a painstaking and long-lasting activity?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree in every respect. Anyone carrying a gun, in a moment of intoxication or diminished mental capacity, could do anything dangerous, and whoever happened to cross his path, be it a member of a brigade, a civilian, or politician, could be in harm's way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was not one such victim the president of the Executive Board of Novo Sarajevo, Udo Obradovic, an excellent man, who was killed by a Serb?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. On the day of his murder, I attended an internal meeting where Mr. Obradovic was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Krajisnik said: [In English] "Judges have been elected. The authorities started to function and apply these laws. So now in the fourth phase, I expect that authorities start to function completely and that we integrate, during the negotiations, our own nationally constructive identity." [Interpretation] So the fourth stage where it is expected to be fully operational would commence on the 1st of January, 1995, and not sooner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? And I suppose that we will take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted as Exhibit D1245. And we'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please conclude by half past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 10876.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, Mr. Prstojevic: Tell us, what was the situation like with regard to water and electricity supply in Ilidza and other areas?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, you need to know the issue thoroughly. The water sources for Ilidza originate in the mountains, with the natural fall of the water, and in the underground wells in Ilidza, where water needs to be pumped out at a certain feature, at Mojmilo, as well as at certain water-pump stations in Sarajevo which would take it from there. Let me tell you that some of the wells at Ilidza were under Serb control, two or three were at Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica, and one was at Stup, under the HVO control. Right from the start, the Muslims would re-siphon the wells at Kolonija and Mojmilo for their own purposes, which is easily done, and Vojkovici and Grlica, which are neighbourhoods of Ilidza, would start -- would actually no longer have water as of April of that year. So the population had to resort to other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at this document, where, as reasons for the suspension of water supply, was mentioned the constant shelling of Ilidza. And due to the shelling, the water supply system has been damaged at the pumping station and well site at Bacevo, et cetera. So was this the main reason, specifically shelling of transformer stations and pumping stations, behind the lack of water?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have before me is the water grid of Ilidza. The pumping station was some 200 metres away from the Command of the Crisis Staff, which was later to become the Command of the Ilidza Brigade. It was frequently shelled, and this was also one of the reasons why the staff could not reach their work-place frequently. There were only two occasions when there was electricity, and both the Serbian and the Muslim areas would have water. In all the other circumstances where the electricity was not available, nobody would have water because it couldn't be pumped. The brigadier general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... in his book, "The Defence of Sarajevo," confessed that throughout the war they received their water supplies from Jahorina, where our leadership was located, because there was the natural fall of water. They also received water from Tilava, which was under the command of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade in the area of the responsibility of the Ilidza Battalion of Kasindol. And this is what he had to say about Ilidza, and I'm quoting: "When these water sources didn't have electricity," and thus disabling the system, "the town would have no water." But he admitted that the town was lucky to have these wells because there was underground water, so they didn't have any problems. But that particular date, the 4th of August, 1992, several days later the Muslims would launch a fierce offensive against us and have heavy losses. This was the 31st of July and the 4th of August, and they would sustain the highest losses on these two dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have much time. I have to move on.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just tell you, there was a fierce attack on Vojkovici and Ilidza on this day when everything was damaged and destroyed. I think the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1246, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3083, please. It's the 27th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your director of the public utility company is informing you about the waterworks situation. There is a reference to electricity, problems with central heating. He says that the pipes are half empty and have, therefore, frozen and are broken now. Can we have the next page, please. So there are many breakdowns. It is impossible to clean the clogged pipes. And on the next page, it says that many problems were dealt with, but on that very day, they have 300 breakdowns that were reported. He is complaining that a lot of water is being wasted when the pipes break down. Do you remember having received this information from the director of the public utilities company?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and I have the original of that report here with me. But I have to tell you more about the 4th of August. UNPROFOR was informed, and the breakdown was repaired within the shortest period of time possible. I think that by the 12th of August, according to my records, it was supposed to be repaired. This report is a professional and accurate report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1247, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5305 briefly, please. P5305 [as interpreted], please. P2305. It has been admitted as a P document, and the 65 ter number is 1658.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a report here from our State Security Service in Ilidza, and there are still problems with Brne. You see what the second paragraph says; that when the new commander arrived, Colonel Cajic, Brne's formation felt it would not have the privileges it had had until then, and they were even getting ready to assassinate him. There is another reference here to the effect that the leadership had ordered their re-subordination and that they did not want to be re-subordinated; that they are bad-mouthing people. Brne says, for instance, that former JNA officers are a bunch of incompetents, whereas Captain Dragan, Arkan, and he personally are the only ones who are of any use. Then there is slander of members of the MUP, and so on and so forth. Does this correspond to the situation as it was ? Yes, I read this out too fast. It should be pointed out that, likewise, they were bothered by the civilian authorities, as well as officials of the MUP concerning whom they are saying various things that are untrue, slandering them, saying that they are thieves, criminals, and so on. Is that the situation with this small group that is just lying around in Rakovica and behaving as if they were a foreign body?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. This group of some 20 men, although others overestimated because they don't have accurate information, they did not want to be under the command of the Igman Brigade, but that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have that old 65 ter number now, 07177, your testimony of the 15th of June, 2005. So 07177, and then page 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your answer that starts with the words: "Well, I don't know ..." I don't have to read all of it out. And you're speaking up until line 11, and you're saying that some groups mentioned at the beginning of a particular telephone intercept, Brne's group, Balkan's group, they only came to Ilidza briefly, as well as some Chetniks from Zvornik, from Republika Srpska. Arkan's group spent two or three days there. And you say: [In English] "But we were not in [indiscernible] their presence, and they left Ilidza very quickly. I cannot tell you the exact date now, but I believe that I have told you at same point ..." [Interpretation] Is this correct, this -- what was said in relation to these groups?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me just a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We really haven't got any time.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the Prosecutor took advantage of a particular section. He took something out of context to say that I brought people from outside, but this is what I said previously: We were not bringing people from elsewhere, from outside. Generally speaking, we were not. I heard that part on the CD the other day. I have this here in front of me. And then he asked me, Who are these people from elsewhere, it has to do with that conversation with this other man -- Arkan's group, Brne's group and Balkan's group, and not a single group was there at that point in time. I say quite clearly, But we did not bring people from elsewhere, generally speaking. Again, somebody is translating this and saying: "We were not enthralled." I said, I never worked with any of these people. I never asked for any of these people. As a rule, they came of their own free will as an evil. This is what it says in my interview from 2005 [Realtime transcript read in error "1995"], "as an evil." Ilidza was strong. We did not need these groups.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 2005. It is not 1995. There is a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2005.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 54 in this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what you say here: "I think there was no need for any special decision, in fact." [In English] "Who took this decision in Ilidza? Who imposed to these paramilitaries to re-subordinate to the Army of RS?" [Interpretation] This is what you say: That there was no need for any special decision; that there were pre-existent rules and regulations with regard to mobilisation, and that referred to all of the population: "Everybody had to be either encompassed by the military units or within the MUP, or they had to be under the so-called work obligations." Is that what you said then?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and now I confirm. According to the mobilisation rules within the federal regulations that were in force, volunteers had to be part of TO units or military units. What I have here with me is the commander -- is the order of the commander of the Ilidza Brigade of the 25th of May to the effect that military conscripts and volunteers are sent to the commands of brigades in order to receive uniforms and to be deployed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could these two pages be added to that other document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's better to admit one page previous, i.e., from T-14546 to 14522 in its entirety. It's not very long, just six or seven pages, and one page is just blank. I take it there's no position on your part, Mr. Tieger, to admit those six or seven pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted -- added to the previous exhibit, 1221.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have P1483, General Mladic's diary, page 182 both in Serbian and in English. The typewritten version in Serbian, please. P1483, on the 2nd of June, 1993, the meeting between the representatives of the government and the commanders and organs of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. So it is page 182.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now have a look at this. Galic says: "There are blockaded forces in Sarajevo. The 1st Muslim Corps (11 brigades - around 40.000," he says, "Turks)." Was that our objective, for them to be blockaded, not for us to take Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what General Mladic meant. However, I know something else. We never tried to take Sarajevo, and there is no order to that effect, as far as the part of Ilidza is concerned. Secondly, from the 1st Corps, they could already send troops out through the airport, those that would act in co-ordination with Tactical Group South and the 3rd Corps and the Podrinska Brigade, and attack from the outside, attack Serb Sarajevo from the outside.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please, let us have the next page, page 183, where it says that the problems are poor supplies, moving out, paramilitaries; right? You see here at the top. "... poor supply, moving away, paramilitaries." And then can we have page 185. 185, Prstojevic says: "Co-operation with all four brigades at a very high level." Already at that point in time until February -- no, until June 1993, you have 553 dead and 1.876 wounded, excluding civilian casualties. Can we now have page 190, please, 190 from this document, both in Serbian and in English. The president of Novo Sarajevo says the municipal numbers around 30.000 people, including 1.500 Muslims and 200 Croats, and he complains: "We are constantly exposed to sniper fire coming from the right bank of the Miljacka River, Mojmilo, Asimovo, and Debelo Brdo." Can we have 191, the next page. The president of the Assembly, Krajisnik, says: "That is the most difficult front." And Mladic is saying that it's wrong that the military do not have IDs. And he's saying: "How can there be any paramilitary formation in the territory of Sarajevo? Paramilitaries are never going to bring freedom." The next page both in Serbian and in English: "They will never bring freedom, and criminals cannot create a state."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this meeting of the Sarajevo municipalities and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. But you see, practically, paramilitaries are formally under the command, but every now and then they do something apart from the command that is not referred to in their orders, and that is why there is this reference to paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Serb municipality of Ilidza, in the government there, was there a person called Dragisa Dragisic? Was there any official in the government there called Dragisa Dragisic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not in the government, not in the SDS of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 30766 to see who it was that called groups to come to Ilidza. 65 ter 30766. This is a conversation between some Valter - this is obviously a conspiratorial name - and Legija, and then an unknown man, and then Zeljko Raznatovic and Legija. Can we have the next page, please. The last entry or reply states Legija says: "Everything --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not see where that was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please. It's not in the transcript because of the speed, and then the document will be tendered anyway. So he says what was promised or what was said did not pass, so he had to organise on his own. And then it states: "He did not link us up with anybody ." And that he called the Crisis Staff himself; that it was disorganised, there's lack of discipline: "As soon as the first casualties occurred, everything became completely disorganised and discipline broke down." Can we have the next page, please. It says that he was completely encircled there. The next page in the Serbian here, it says: "He never connected us with anybody." Can we have the next page. He was encircled, there were wounded, and that in the middle of battle, he says: "These hicks stole their vehicle and escaped from the front." Can we have the next page, please. It says here that it's that vehicle, and then it says here that: "You cannot ..." And then he curses. When you take him to battle, he gets to his house. And then he says: "I am proceeding no further. My house has been liberated." And then it goes on with a swear word of some sort, and then it continues. He talks about Juka and taking prisoners, and then he says: "Yesterday, I had --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We do not see the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's impossible to follow. What is your question? And I see the time. Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's my question: This Dragisa Dragisic, and we will see that here, some Dragisa Dragisic, called them. This is, let's say on -- first of all, on the next page, it says that the chief of the SUP did not allow anything to happen to those prisoners. He said: "These are neighbours ..." And so on and so forth. Well, if we get the next page, we are going to see that; in the English as well. And then on page ERN 0329-0475, it says that Dragisa Dragisic, who had called them and promised, did not keep -- make good on his promise and that they did not manage to make any connections. Did these people appear completely without any connections to you, as is indicated by this telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely correct, but I think this is Dragisa Ivilja [phoen] that is involved here, who was not under any kind of control by the police even before the war. It's not true that he had 100 prisoners in the place where there was battle underway. This could be something else. This group completely came along private lines, just like all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Some witnesses here mentioned that there was some private arrangements and so on. So that is what you mean, isn't it, when you say that definitely this Dragisa did not represent any kind of authorities in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. He was not under the control of the Ilidza authorities before the war. This also refers to Sinisa Ilic, called Monga [phoen]. I know this from the government, from the Assembly, before the war. These are people who belong to the Ilidza underground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At 0329-0476, it says: "It went well for a couple of days before there was shooting." Does that mean they had come a few days before the firing, tried to organise some kind of training? He says: "We tried to organise some training." And then: "There was lack of organisation. Even Serbs were firing at each other." And then already Zeljko Raznatovic is speaking here. He repeats: "Yes. When they come to their house," he says, "I have defended my house, I'm not going any further." Was this also something that used to happened?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came on the 12th, in the evening. On the 13th, they were going all over Ilidza. On the 14th, Sarajevo attacked us. They took part in the fighting. And then after the 15th, I don't know anything about them. This is what Territorial Defence battling meant, battling in front of your own house.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we now tender this, please? And then you can identify the areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1248, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, I haven't heard from you on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't going to enter into the intercept, but I was concerned about the encroachment on the time that was allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I rely on his statement that this is going to be his last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D0 -- 1D1088. This is a map. I'm sorry that we are not able to show you other maps for the Trial Chamber to be able to see where the lines went along your streets and between houses, but we are going to do that at some other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this map, Mr. Prstojevic, and do the blue areas represent Serb-populated neighbourhoods, the green ones Muslim-inhabited areas, and the ochre-yellow Croat-inhabited areas?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is Hrasnica, shown here, as being under the control of the Muslim Army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you continue: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I guess I just prematurely arose after what was apparently the last question, but apparently the questions continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I wanted to say was:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this correctly shown, how the neighbourhoods with Serb, Muslim and Croat majorities indicate that it is mostly the Serbs who controlled the Serbian neighbourhoods and the Muslims who controlled the Muslim neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the first part of the witness's answer because the speakers were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Prstojevic? The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered in the affirmative. Hrasnica was under Muslim control and has a wide exit towards Igman, which you can see. However, this map is of a very large scale. You would need to have a military scale of 1:100.000 ratio where you could see streets where Serbs were on one side and Muslims on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please put your signature and today's date on this map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It won't be necessary. He didn't mark anything. We cannot admit it as is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he identified the map as saying that the colours of the neighbourhoods correspond to the lines of the fronts and that we can see how the lines lie in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I did mark that on other maps. I have better maps on me right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said it can be admitted as it is, without the witness having to sign this document. I don't think we need a translation. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1249, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, I'd like to begin with an issue that was raised by the accused at approximately page 33 today, and that was in connection with a portion of your testimony during the Krajisnik case that began on transcript page 14631. And he read out to you a portion that derived from the question: "Well, if they weren't being expelled in any organised fashion, then in what fashion were they being expelled?" And then you went on to describe that in the areas that -- where combat activities were being conducted, that Muslims were driven out, et cetera. Now, that conversation, Mr. Prstojevic, continued. And as we -- there was a further discussion about Bascarsija, another question about detainees and so on. But when we get to page 14635 of that testimony, it continued: "With respect to the position on how to deal with the situation where combat activities emerge, was that your decision or a decision taken at higher levels and passed on to you?" You stated to the effect that when combat activities emerged, things took their course. The decisions were not taken individually, but rather by collective bodies; in this particular case, by the Crisis Staff. You said it was a tumultuous period. On the next page, the Judge asked you to respond to the question, rather than provide a lot of things. Then the Judge asked you the question about what you said in a previous -- about a previous intercept in which you were a participant and in which you said: "I have a decision from before." And he asked: "What was that decision from before?" And you said at first: "I don't know which decision is being referred to." The Judge said: "Nevertheless, you just told us what the subject of the decision was. It was about the position." And he said: "That suggests you know more about the decision, as you're telling us now." You said: "That's precisely why I was telling you this. The war situation dictated the moves to be taken ..." And so on. And then continuing on to 14637, the Judge continued to press you about that, saying he understood that decisions have to be taken, but that's not a decision from before. That refers to a decision that had already been taken. You said: "You have to understand what I'm saying. We had taken certain views and positions to enable us to know how to react in a given situation, because we would have failed entirely had we not known what to do when." The Judge asked -- you said at some point you couldn't recall precisely what they were, they were not in written form. The Judge said: "Would that include expelling the population, including the civilian population?" You said: "It would mean that the population had to be moved out if the entire area was under a threat, or if it meant that the entire area would be lost to the enemy, or if it meant that the population would be in grave danger. This is precisely what happened in Kotorac, which was mentioned in yesterday's intercept." The Judge asked: "Do I understand that if circumstances required you to do so, that you would remove the civilian population from the area?" You said: "Yes, but that meant that both the Serbian and Muslim populations were moved out, and this also meant that the -- and the Croats as well, and the population itself would move out on their own initiative." Mr. Prstojevic, those were your -- that was your testimony in 2005, specifically, June 16th, 2005, in the course of responding to the question that the accused initially brought your attention to; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but this actually is where you put some 10 or 15 questions. As for the intercept of the 14th of June between myself and Dragan Lubura, when there was a horrendous offensive by Muslim forces in that area, because they had already captured certain sections of Ilidza, I never used the term "protirivanje" [phoen], "to expel." And this is all right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've been explaining for over 18 hours now. I have very few minutes to ask you a few questions. You confirmed my question. Your Honour, I would tender these pages, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, do we have an intercept in which Mr. Prstojevic allegedly had said: "I have a decision from before"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that that question was in response to what is now P1492, Your Honour, in the context. And I'm happy to tender the pages relating to that, but I believe that that is -- that that was in connection with his testimony in relation to that intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's as part of P1494?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we up-load it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The particular passage is Mr. Prstojevic: "Well, what should we do? Would it be good if we gave it a thought and if we organised people from outside to expel them all. Nobody needs to be shot or killed. Everybody expelled." And then he continues -- that's after his interlocutor says: "That would be the right move." And he continues: "That is a bit -- let's say that you make preparations. I have a decision from before." And that's what the reference in these pages is to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In our case, P1492. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, an intercept dated the 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll add those pages to the existing Prosecution exhibit. Do we have a separate number for the Prosecution? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was it? P2513.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to move next to a discussion that took place around pages 59 through 60 or so of today's testimony, Mr. Prstojevic, and that's a discussion of the conversation that you had with Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I get -- may I get a chance to explain the term "protirivanje" and the decision before that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you explained several times before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It has been the subject of testimony already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never used the word "protirivate" [phoen], "to expel." The decision is in my head. Where we have battle or fighting, we know what we need to do, from the military point of view, from the military aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we have the intercept and the audio in evidence, and that can be listened to extensively, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, turning to the intercept of the 2nd of June, you testified today, Mr. Prstojevic, that you insisted -- you said to Mr. Mandic: "Where did I say that?" And then you also added that: "The investigators proceeded along their own track." In fact, that was the subject of testimony during the Krajisnik case as well, during which you were asked a number of questions about that intercept. First, your attention was brought -- and this is beginning at page 14644. You were asked about Mandic's comment that his attention is brought and the attention of the government is brought to the fact you were issuing ultimatums to some Turks, evicting people from certain settlements and so on. You said you denied it to the minister right away. And moving on to page 14645, you were asked whether you understood that Mr. Mandic was calling because he wanted Musanovic to be put in a position so it could be publicised. You said that's the way you understood it. You were asked about Mandic further understanding that you were evicting people from certain settlements, and then expressing concern about the publicity that was bringing. You said you didn't think he was concerned one bit. Then the question was put: "Looking at the intercept, in particular," and you were confronted with the fact that you then tell him: "We didn't say it, not in public." And then again you say: "Well, we didn't say it in public, nor did we write it." And then you were asked: "So you're assuring Mr. Mandic, are you not, that there shouldn't be any bad publicity because there's nothing public about it?" And then you say -- you said to Mandic: "Please, where did I say such a thing? I don't know. We never said that publicly. This is not our policy." That continues until the Judges intervene and focus your attention on the fact that you said "not in public." And that's Judge Hanoteau speaking at pages 14647, 14648. That's not the investigators. And Judge Hanoteau says: "So this is what you're saying." This is at page 14648: "We did not say that, not in public. We did not say that, not in public." So it seems that you're saying is that you said it, but not in public. And then, in fact, the next sentence, this is what you say: "We did not say that in public." And you continue until page -- talking about a number of other things, including what happened in Kotorac and expelling civilians in areas where circumstances require the population to leave, or where the population want to leave on their own initiative, and then you begin the answer from Judge Hanoteau by say: "As for the part where I say that we did not say it in public, had this been written or said in public, this would have been disseminated by the media and it would have disturbed the general public ..." Et cetera. And finally Judge Orie also presses you about -- to please explain at what point you flatly deny that evictions took place in this telephone conversation. You say -- well, on this same page, after this long intervention where I say: "Well, yes, but please tell me, wherever did I say this?" And Judge Orie says, according to a logical interpretation, after quoting you: "You are denying that you said that you are not responsible for their safety or something else. It's not a denial of any conversation occurring." And he asks you to comment, and you say, in your conversation with the minister, you focus him, saying that: "We had issued an ultimatum to the Muslims in a settlement that they were to move out within 24 hours, and that's what I focused on, and I was denying that." Mr. Prstojevic -- and there's a bit more, but it's on that same page of 14650. Mr. Prstojevic, that is a reflection of your responses to the -- to questions raised about the 2 June intercept with Mr. Mandic during the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. An ultimatum was not broadcast anywhere. I'm not a trumpeter to climb up on a hill and announce this or that. I explained this speech precisely in 2003. Fadil Musanovic is alive. He can be called as a witness. At that time, we did not interfere in the work of the judiciary. I keep saying if Mr. Mandic knows, where does he know that from? And this is why I was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You had a chance to explain that during the course of this testimony. I'm now tendering what you said in the Krajisnik case as well. It will be before the Court. Your Honour, if we could have those pages added, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, as -- could you identify the transcript page numbers, Mr. Tieger? It's from 14645 to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. From 146 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness denied the accuracy of what was written and how it was understood. He does not accept that as his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Accuracy of the transcript can be checked in other ways. We'll admit this, and this will be added to P2513.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we move on, could you give the exhibit number of that intercept of 2nd of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's 1011 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1110.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Prstojevic, earlier in your testimony, specifically on Friday, you were asked by the accused, at page 13646, about agreements. And you said there -- you were asked the question -- excuse me. You were actually taken to an earlier -- earlier comments you had made from earlier testimony about agreements, and you said there was political activity in Bosnia aimed at seeking a peaceful solution. The Ilidza leadership went along with that: "No matter what kind of agreement could be reached by our leaders, we would have accepted it." Et cetera. And you indicated that you stood by what you said. I wanted to now direct your attention to 65 ter 07875, and that's a portion of an interview that took place in 2003. That's contained at page -- beginning at page 10 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S. The question was asked: "How did you receive the information in relation to the policies that you were meant to apply in Ilidza?" You said: "Mostly there were certain meetings, and that one meeting, if you -- if you don't remember well, you also asked me when the second phase -- when the local phase was to be activated, a discussion about that meeting before." You continue on to the next page. That's page 11: "I will say only one sentence about it. I understood at that meeting, there was a lot of -- at that meeting, there was a lot of threatening rhetoric, like if we cannot agree and we cannot find an agreement, he will do this, this and this, and I'm sorry to use this word, but we'll fuck their mother, and this last word, in particular, I mentioned because I heard it and I remembered it well, and the relations or balance were 50:50. And who will be destroyed, it was not known. It was relative." And you were asked, after you said that, when you heard those words you quoted, was it your understanding that then it was the case of the ethnicity being imposed and one being destroyed, and you said: "In essence, this should not be understood that -- that roughly, but, in essence, it's division by hook or by crook or in a peaceful manner, or by force." And then you continued. You were asked: "Did you understand that the goal was to -- that after that meeting, that the goal was to achieve ethnic separation by any means?" And you said at page 12: "Exactly in that way if they don't find the solution or agreement. But since we were dissatisfied with that, we did not take certain steps to implement things, but naturally the time will cause things to happen." And then it moves on to a discussion of the strategic objectives which I may refer your attention to in a moment. Mr. Prstojevic, that was a reflection of your discussion in 2003 concerning the issue of agreement or what might happen if no agreement was reached; correct? And that was on the 27th of November, 2003.

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it is you're asking me here. What was the date of the meeting that we had over coffee, Markovic -- where we were informed at a meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's what you said to investigators about that issue when you spoke to them in 2003; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDJELJKO PRSTOJEVIC [Resumed]
